questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes entropy from cross-entropy for discrete distributions?
questions.choice_A: Entropy H(P) measures the expected code length under P for data drawn from P, while cross-entropy H(P, Q) measures the expected code length when encoding data drawn from P using a code optimized for Q.
questions.choice_B: Entropy H(P) is the same as the negative log-likelihood, while cross-entropy H(P, Q) is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.
questions.choice_C: Entropy H(P) depends on both P and Q, while cross-entropy H(P, Q) depends only on P.
questions.choice_D: Entropy is only defined for continuous variables, while cross-entropy is only defined for discrete variables.

questions.question: Which equality links cross-entropy, entropy, and KL divergence for distributions P and Q over the same support (discrete case)?
questions.choice_A: H(P, Q) = KL(Q || P) + H(Q)
questions.choice_B: H(P, Q) = H(P) + KL(P || Q)
questions.choice_C: H(P, Q) = KL(P || Q) - H(P)
questions.choice_D: H(P, Q) = H(Q) - KL(P || Q)

questions.question: Why can KL(P || Q) be infinite even when both P and Q are valid probability distributions?
questions.choice_A: Because KL requires both distributions to be Gaussian.
questions.choice_B: Because if Q assigns zero probability to an event that P assigns positive probability, the log-density ratio diverges.
questions.choice_C: Because KL requires the same entropy for P and Q.
questions.choice_D: Because KL is undefined for discrete distributions.

questions.question: Which property is true of the Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(P || Q) for probability distributions over the same space?
questions.choice_A: It is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality.
questions.choice_B: It is always less than or equal to 1.
questions.choice_C: It is non-negative and equals zero if and only if P = Q almost everywhere.
questions.choice_D: It is concave in Q for fixed P.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the relationship between maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and cross-entropy?
questions.choice_A: MLE maximizes entropy of the model distribution.
questions.choice_B: MLE minimizes KL(P || Q) where Q is the data distribution and P is the model.
questions.choice_C: MLE minimizes empirical cross-entropy of the data distribution with respect to the model.
questions.choice_D: MLE maximizes the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the data and the model.

questions.question: In the context of variational inference for Bayesian models, the evidence lower bound (ELBO) typically contains which KL term?
questions.choice_A: KL(p(θ|x) || q(θ)) to encourage q to cover all modes of the posterior.
questions.choice_B: KL(q(θ) || p(θ|x)) which is tractable to compute exactly.
questions.choice_C: KL(q(θ) || p(θ)) acting as a regularizer that pulls the variational distribution toward the prior.
questions.choice_D: KL(p(θ) || q(θ)) which always equals cross-entropy minus entropy.

questions.question: What is a key difference between differential entropy for continuous variables and KL divergence between continuous densities?
questions.choice_A: Differential entropy is invariant under invertible reparameterizations, whereas KL is not.
questions.choice_B: Differential entropy can be negative and is not invariant to reparameterization, whereas KL is invariant under smooth invertible transformations.
questions.choice_C: Both differential entropy and KL are always non-negative and invariant.
questions.choice_D: KL can be negative for continuous variables, whereas differential entropy cannot.

questions.question: Which symmetrized divergence is bounded and often used because it avoids infinite values when supports differ?
questions.choice_A: J-divergence: KL(P || Q) + KL(Q || P), which is always bounded by 1.
questions.choice_B: Jensen–Shannon divergence, which is the average KL to the mixture M = (P + Q)/2 and is bounded between 0 and log 2 (for base-2 logs).
questions.choice_C: Total variation distance, which equals KL(P || Q) + KL(Q || P).
questions.choice_D: Hellinger distance, which is identical to JS divergence.

questions.question: Which practical challenge arises when estimating KL(P || Q) from samples if Q is known only up to a normalizing constant?
questions.choice_A: KL cannot be estimated because the normalizing constant cancels out in all cases.
questions.choice_B: The log-density ratio requires the unknown normalizing constant of Q, so one must use methods like importance sampling or variational bounds that avoid evaluating the constant directly.
questions.choice_C: KL is undefined unless both distributions are normalized exactly.
questions.choice_D: This is not a challenge since the Monte Carlo estimator for KL never needs densities.

questions.question: Why does the direction of KL matter in approximate inference and regularization?
questions.choice_A: Because KL is symmetric only for Gaussian distributions.
questions.choice_B: Minimizing KL(q || p) tends to be mode-seeking, while minimizing KL(p || q) is mode-covering; this affects how approximations handle multimodal targets.
questions.choice_C: The direction only affects computational cost, not qualitative behavior.
questions.choice_D: The direction determines whether the result is a proper distance metric.

questions.question: Which statement about cross-entropy and average negative log-likelihood (NLL) on an i.i.d. dataset is correct?
questions.choice_A: The empirical average NLL of a model equals the empirical cross-entropy between the empirical data distribution and the model.
questions.choice_B: Empirical NLL is always less than the true cross-entropy.
questions.choice_C: Empirical NLL equals the model entropy.
questions.choice_D: Empirical NLL equals KL(model || data) plus model entropy.

questions.question: What is a core reason that KL(P || Q) is often preferred as a regularizer in VAEs with Gaussian latents?
questions.choice_A: It always has a closed form for any pair of distributions.
questions.choice_B: For common choices (e.g., Gaussian q(z|x) and standard normal prior p(z)), the KL term has a closed-form expression, enabling stable and efficient training.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees that the decoder becomes deterministic.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the learned latent variables are independent.

questions.question: Which of the following is a property of KL divergence as an f-divergence?
questions.choice_A: It obeys a data processing inequality: applying a measurable mapping to both distributions cannot increase KL.
questions.choice_B: It equals the Wasserstein-1 distance for all distributions.
questions.choice_C: It is the only divergence that metrizes weak convergence.
questions.choice_D: It is always upper bounded by total variation distance.

questions.question: In practice, why can minibatch estimates of KL terms introduce bias during training?
questions.choice_A: KL is linear in parameters, so any subsampling makes it zero.
questions.choice_B: KL involves expectations of nonlinear functions (e.g., log-density ratios), and moving expectations inside nonlinearities introduces bias with finite samples.
questions.choice_C: Minibatching only affects gradient variance, never bias.
questions.choice_D: KL is invariant to sample size and thus cannot be estimated from minibatches.

questions.question: What happens to cross-entropy H(P, Q) when Q perfectly matches P?
questions.choice_A: It becomes negative infinity.
questions.choice_B: It equals H(Q) and is larger than H(P).
questions.choice_C: It equals H(P).
questions.choice_D: It equals H(P) + H(Q).

questions.question: Which approach allows estimation of KL or other f-divergences from samples by learning a classifier or critic?
questions.choice_A: Kernel density estimation only.
questions.choice_B: k-nearest neighbor plug-in estimators exclusively.
questions.choice_C: Variational characterization using a parameterized critic (e.g., f-GAN, Donsker–Varadhan/MINE-style bounds).
questions.choice_D: Exact computation by Monte Carlo without densities.

questions.question: Which statement about the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) is correct?
questions.choice_A: Its square root defines a metric, and JSD remains finite even when P and Q have disjoint supports.
questions.choice_B: JSD equals twice the total variation distance.
questions.choice_C: JSD is unbounded above.
questions.choice_D: JSD is identical to KL(P || Q) when P and Q are equal.

questions.question: Why is the plug-in estimator of entropy using empirical frequencies biased for finite samples?
questions.choice_A: Because the empirical distribution always underestimates probabilities of rare events, leading to upward bias in entropy.
questions.choice_B: Because entropy is concave in the distribution, making the expected plug-in estimate downward biased (Jensen’s inequality).
questions.choice_C: Because entropy is linear in probabilities, and linear estimators are unbiased.
questions.choice_D: Because the estimator ignores the KL divergence.

questions.question: Which practical consideration is most important when using KL as a regularizer in deep generative models?
questions.choice_A: Ensuring the KL term is maximized to improve coverage.
questions.choice_B: Balancing the reconstruction/likelihood term with the KL term (e.g., with a coefficient like β) to trade off fit and regularization.
questions.choice_C: Replacing the KL with total variation to improve gradients.
questions.choice_D: Setting the KL to zero to avoid posterior collapse.

questions.question: Given only samples from P and Q (with no density access), which statement about estimating KL(P || Q) is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: KL can be exactly computed from samples via Monte Carlo.
questions.choice_B: KL estimation is nontrivial; one must use indirect methods such as density-ratio estimation, kNN estimators, or variational bounds with a learned critic.
questions.choice_C: KL cannot be approximated under any circumstances.
questions.choice_D: KL equals the difference of sample entropies, which is consistent in high dimensions.

questions.question: Which scenario illustrates support mismatch issues in practice and a common workaround?
questions.choice_A: When P is continuous and Q is discrete but with overlapping support, KL is finite; add noise to Q to reduce variance.
questions.choice_B: When P has mass where Q has zero, KL(P || Q) is infinite; practitioners often add smoothing or a small floor to Q to avoid numerical blow-ups during training.
questions.choice_C: When Q dominates P everywhere, KL(Q || P) is always zero; resample data.
questions.choice_D: Support mismatch never affects KL; it only affects total variation.
